explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The psalm says, "The LORD reigns; let the nations tremble!" (Psalm 99:1). Trembling is a lot of things, but it's not lounging on a couch with a cookie. Think of someone who walks into a room and everybody sits up straight. That's the feel here.

Right, baker. The psalm says, "The LORD reigns; let the nations tremble!" (Psalm 99:1). Nobody trembling is also leaning back with their feet up. It's the opposite of a nap. The reign of the LORD gets a big response, and this verse is only the start of it.

That's it, baker. The psalm says, "Great is the LORD in Zion; He is exalted above all the peoples." (Psalm 99:2). All the peoples is a big circle, and nobody gets left outside it. Zion is where He's called great, and the whole world is under that same word.

Close, friend, but the circle is bigger than that. The psalm says He is "…exalted above all the peoples." (Psalm 99:2). That's every people, not just one. Israel is in there, and so is everybody else.

Good guess, since priests show up later in the psalm. But verse 2 says He is "…exalted above all the peoples." (Psalm 99:2). That's way wider than one group. The priests are in there, and so is everybody else.

You've got it, friend. The psalm says, "The mighty King loves justice. You have established equity; You have exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob." (Psalm 99:4). Notice it says justice and righteousness together. I'd keep that pair in my apron pocket.

Not this time, baker. The psalm says, "You have exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob." (Psalm 99:4). So the text says yes, He did. It also says the mighty King loves justice, so this isn't a side detail.

Yes, baker. The psalm says, "Moses and Aaron were among His priests…" (Psalm 99:6). Notice it says "among" His priests, so the psalm isn't saying they were the only two. Two names, and the psalm is just getting warmed up.

Good names, friend, but they're not in this psalm. Zadok was a priest in David's day, along with Ahimelech (2 Samuel 8:17). This psalm says, "Moses and Aaron were among His priests…" (Psalm 99:6). Those are the two it names.
Nice try, baker. Eli was a priest, and Phinehas was one of his sons (1 Samuel 1:3, 9). But the psalm says, "Moses and Aaron were among His priests…" (Psalm 99:6). Those are the two it names.
Yes, friend. The psalm says, "They called to the LORD and He answered." (Psalm 99:6). That's three names and one clear result. Calling and being answered sit right next to each other in that line.
Not quite, baker. The psalm says, "They called to the LORD and He answered." (Psalm 99:6). It's said plainly, with no ifs. And verse 8 says it again, speaking to Him: "…You answered them."
That's it, baker. The psalm says, "they kept His decrees and the statutes He gave them." (Psalm 99:7). He spoke from the pillar of cloud, and they kept what He gave. Simple as that.

Friend, the psalm goes the other way. It says, "they kept His decrees and the statutes He gave them." (Psalm 99:7). Forgetting is more my specialty. I once forgot a whole batch in the oven, and the timer was RIGHT THERE.

Good thought, but that's not what the text says. The psalm says, "they kept His decrees and the statutes He gave them." (Psalm 99:7). Kept is the word. It doesn't say a thing about questioning in that verse.

explanations.answer: Forgiving yet an avenger of their misdeeds
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says, "You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds." (Psalm 99:8). Both halves are in the same verse, and it keeps both. Don't drop either one.

explanations.answer: Forgiving so He overlooked their misdeeds
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. It says, "You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds." (Psalm 99:8). That "yet" matters. The psalm doesn't say He overlooked anything.

explanations.answer: Strict so He never forgave their misdeeds
explanations.explanation: Half of it is in there, baker, but not all of it. The psalm says, "You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds." (Psalm 99:8). Forgiving comes first in that line. So "never forgave" doesn't match the text.

Yes, baker. The psalm ends, "Exalt the LORD our God and worship at His holy mountain…" (Psalm 99:9). Verse 5 said to worship at His footstool, and now the call is to worship at His holy mountain. The word that closes the call is mountain.

Nice guess, friend, but there's no river in this psalm. The last call is, "Exalt the LORD our God and worship at His holy mountain…" (Psalm 99:9). The word is mountain. I'd have loved a river by the bakery, but the psalm doesn't give me one.
Pretty picture, baker, but it's not the word. The psalm says, "…worship at His holy mountain…" (Psalm 99:9). Mountain is how the psalm closes the call. No gardens in these nine verses.
